Canadian National Railways
Tour committee has had under consideration item 408 of the estimates, which provides for loans or guarantees of $22,500,000 of the Canadian National Railway Company for the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1928, and has in the course of its deliberations, examined the operating statements of the company for the year ending December 31st, 1926.
(Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
Your committee notes that the results of the operations of the Canadian National Railway System, which includes for the first time the operations of the Central Vermont Railway, show a substantial improvement in the volume of business handled and a continued improvement in operating methods, resulting in an increase of $21,861,000 in operating revenue accompanied by an increase of only $7,079,000 in operating expenses.
While not providing for interest charges due the government on capital advances your committee notes with considerable satisfaction that for the first time, the net earnings of the railway for the year are more than sufficient to pay all fixed charges due to the public.
Your committee is lead to believe that the properties embraced in the system have been maintained to a standard commensurate with the traffic requirements.
Your committee agrees that the estimate of $22,500,000 (being a reduction of $8,500,000 from the amount asked for last year) is necessary for the purpose of the company during the coming year, and should be voted by the House.
Canadian Government Merchant Marine
Your committee has also had under consider-ition item 409 of the estimates, which provides tor a loan of $18,500 to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, and has in the course of its deliberations examined the operating statements of the company for the year [DOT] ending December 31st, 1926. YTour committee notes with considerable satisfaction that the operating deficit has been reduced to $90,159, an improvement over the previous year of $858,893, and it is recalled that the improvement in 1925 in comparison with 1924 was $492,826.
From the evidence given, it appears that there has been an improvement in the earnings on the business handled in the ease of practically all the routes operated and that this improvement has been accomplished at a relatively small expense. The increase in operating revenue was $1,114,735, while the operating expenses only increased $256,841.
Your committee draws attention to the fact that the amount of the appropriation for last year on account of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, was $600,000, whereas for the coming year, the sum of $18,500 is asked. Your committee is of the opinion that this amount is necessary for the purposes of the company during the coming year and should be voted by the House.
Your committee notes with satisfaction that the Canadian National Railways continues to hold the confidence and goodwill of the public through the excellence of the service rendered and the courtesy extended to patrons.
Your committee further desires to express its appreciation of the manner in which the President of the Canadian National Railways and the officers assisting him gave their evidence to the committee.
A copy is attached hereto of the minutes of the proceedings and evidence of the attending officers.

Harbour Commissioners' Acts
Your committee further recommends that its proceedings and the evidence adduced before the committee be printed as an appendix to the Journals of the House and that rule 74 in respect hereto be suspended.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

Employment of Amputation Cases in City Post Offices
The above matter was discussed with representatives of the Civil Service Commission and a representative of the Great War Veterans' Association. The following were present:
P. T. Coolican, General Superintendent of Postal Service; E. J. Underwood, Chief Superintendent of Post Office Service; C. H. Bland, Assistant Secretary, Civil Service Commission; Mr. Bouchard, Examination Branch, Civil Service Commission; Mr. Herwig, Great War Veterans' Association.
The department's views were expressed as follows:
The department has no objection to the employment of amputation cases in those positions where their physical handicap does not prevent their giving the department satisfactory service.
The department at the present time has so many employees who are not 100 per cent physically fit in the operating branches of the service, including a large number of men of advanced years who have entered under the returned soldiers' preference, that to further load down these staffs with amputation cases
IMr. E. J. Garland.]
would simply mean that the department could not give an efficient service.
It was pointed out at the interview that the department had no objection to the employment of amputation cases in such positions as mechanical operators in the Money Order branch, telephone operators, stenographers and other similar clerical positions.
It was further stated that the department would assist in every way possible in obtaining properly qualified amputation cases for such positions. This attitude was satisfactory to both the commission and Mr. Herwig of the Great War Veterans' Association and it was agreed that the department would, as far as possible, when suitable vacancies occurred, to which amputation cases could be assigned, to specially draw such cases to the attention of the Civil Service Commission when asking for vacancies to be filled.
I beg to lay the memorandum on the table.

Since when did we desire to place our imprimatur upon favouring agitators of that character? All we -are doing outside of the Criminal Code now is simply to say that we are not going to the trouble of having a long trial and all the accompanying agitation in the public press, magnifying these men into heroes. No, we are merely going to send them back to the country they came from; that is all.
Take the United States of America. They talk of liberty and freedom, and practise it, they say, more than any other people in the world. Would they permit the repeal of a section such as that? Look at the deportations from that country now. Look at the Canadians they have sent back. Look at England refusing to vise passports for certain persons wanting to enter the United States. Look at the action of the United States with respect to undesirables at Ellis Island and at other points.
Why repeal this section now when the 'effect of it is simply to enable us at a moment of great peril, when we are sure of our facts, to send these undesirable persons back to the country they came from? I do submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the time to repeal it. I can see no reason why the government having discharged its duty, as I understand it, to the hon. gentleman, having promised to do something and having done it, should any longer press this legislation in 1927 upon the attention of this House in the closing days of the session, for I know hon. gentlemen opposite are quite as desirous as I am of maintaining law and order in Canada, and are quite as desirous as I am of maintaining our institutions and our form of government, quite as desirous as anyone on this side of the House that there should be orderly and regulated conduct of the business of this country. Then why remove from the Immigration Act this provision.
My friend from Winnipeg, I suppose, would say that the Criminal Code gives us ample opportunity to deal, with these men, but that is the very thing we do not want to use. The United States has found that out by experience, and she simply deports them, instead of exalting these people into heroes, with all the talk about freedom of speech and deporting people without giving them the opportunity of a trial by a jury of their countrymen. That is not the principle of

the law at all. Deportation is not punishment. The criminal law is in operation for the punishment of the offender, and for deterring others; it is to punish those who violate our laws. But deiportation is to send out of our country undesirable citizens, and when this House votes to repeal a section such as that, indirectly it says that it is satisfied that thiaJt class of person is not an undesirable person. To retain the section cannot do harm: it may do good. It cannot interfere with liberty, because it does not deal with British subjects, and since when did an alien have any right to protection in this country other than to be protected in his life and property, and be sent out of the country if he proved undesirable? How many people are sent out of the United States as undersirable? How many are sent out of Russia and other countries? Why should Canada repeal this section which enables us to deal with these people? That is a question I leave with the minister, and I cannot think for a single moment that he is serious in asking us to repeal a section such as this which gives us this protection-a protection that can be put into operation without recourse to the courts of law, with all the costs that go with criminal trials, and all the effort that is made to magnify into heroes these people who would destroy our institutions, and all the talk about the poor stranger and the foreigner within our gates. It is not that. This is merely the exercise of the high right of sovereignty with respect to the citizenship of Canada. It is merely saying that we as a people will keep without our borders undesirable persons who are promulgating these doctrines; that is all, and I do submit that the bill Should not pass.

It is therefore not a matter of mere academic interest, and that is why some of us feel so strongly about it. It was definitely decided by the

I come now to another important consideration. Some of us in this House have been accused again and again of a desire to foster crime simply because we want to get rid of this act. We are charged with wanting to encourage offences of this description and to help people tear down the constitution. I am not advocating any of the things that are legislated against in this act. any of the organizations mentioned. That is too great a power to confer upon any department. If any one is suspected or is even guilty of any such offence the very least we can do is to give him a fair trial and not decide his fate by a departmental investigation. That is what we plead for. As a British citizen I claim for all British born citizens in Canada the right to fair trial by jury.	But I would extend that plea
in the case of those of foreign birth. The leader of the opposition is mistaken, and I would call to his attention the fact that it was the hon. member for West Calgary who last year suggested an amendment to the bill by which he thought to perfect it, which went further than the original draft act as presented by the minister. In the original bill there was some provision for deportation after trial for crimes of this character, but owing to the amendment introduced by the hon. member for West Calgary, that was modified and it was suggested that the whole clause should be eliminated; anyone who was present at the debate last year will recall the change.
My plea, Mr. Speaker, is that the Immigration Act quite rightly undertakes to stand guard at our gates and to say who may be admitted into Canada. If by any chance some get inside our gates who are undesirable I claim that the right still exists under the Immigration Act to deport them. It is perhaps quite in place that the department should have some act on the statute books to permit of such deportation. But so far as I have any influence, I refuse to allow an act to remain on the statute books which will use the departmental machinery for trying a man, and then deporting him without a fair jury trial; I think that is against all our best traditions. Personally I would not object to the country deporting a man who is undesirable; I will go that far with the hon. member for West Calgary. If a man is convicted of belonging to the undesirable classes; if he is convicted of acting against the best interests of Canada, I do not know that I would have any objection to deporting him.

It is not the deportation I object to, and I want to make that quite clear. What I do object to is the deportation without any other trial than that afforded by a departmental investigation.
Mr- HANSON:	Would the hon. member
permit a question? Does he know that under the law of fhe United States on this very point it is always a departmental matter, and that it is the same in England and in every other civilized country? Where does he get the trial by jury on this particular point?

I do not think
the American laws provide for the deportation of American citizens. Our law goes much beyond that; the United States will deport people who are not American citizens, but we undertake to deport Canadian citizens of other than Canadian birth, even those born in Great Britain. I happened to be born in Canada and am not liable under this act; the hon. member who asked the question (Mr. Hanson) is not liable under it, but there are some twenty or thirty men in this House who would come under it, and simply because I happened to be bom in Canada I would not insist upon the right of trial by jury for myself and refuse that right to my fellow Canadian citizens who were so unfortunate as to have been bom in the motherland. It seems to me that the least we can claim is the same rights for the British-born in this country as we claim for our own Canadian-born. We have heard much of equal status. This is equal status, if you like. It seems to me that the House has been labouring for several years under a misapprehension as to the real purposes for which the amendments have been sought. I confess that the bill is a very tricky one, and that it is only by carefully comparing the different sections that one can understand all its bearings. The outstanding feature before us, however, is whether or not British born and foreign born Canadian citizens will have the right to trial by the regular courts before they may be subject to deportation.

speechtext:
He gave way to me for a
few moments, since I am leaving the city shortly. There is a great deal to be said against deportation merely on suspicion. As it now stands, the act might very well be reconsidered, but to repeal it would leave this country in a very precarious condition.
In 1918 I happened to be Director of Public Safety for Canada, and I saw the entire workings of the American, British and Canadian secret services. In that year there were hundreds and thousands of dollars, and I would say up to a million and more, of Russian money brought into this country for the purpose of carrying on an agitation advocating assassination and everything else against which this act purports to enact measures for the protection of the country. I personally sent for the Russians, the communistic emissaries, and had several personal conversations with them, in which I told them very pilainly that any remedial measures which could be adopted by means of order in council at that time would be enacted to prevent their efforts from being carried to the treasonable extent to which they proposed to go. In a measure, by such intimidation we prevented them from carrying out certain measures which they were endeavouring to accomplish by the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars in this country.
The act as it then stood did not go far enough to protect the interests of Canada at that time. I believe this act was drawn up the year after the close of the war; possibly it goes a little too far, but it should not be abrogated, because the same measures are being taken by soviet propaganda in this country to-day. We who know the inside of things are all aware of it; the Department of Justice of Canada must be well advised with regard to it. The efforts which were made in 1918 were successful to a certain extent, but following the close of the war similar efforts have been carried on and are being carried on throughout the length and breadth of this country. If I remember rightly in 1918 there were two secret printing presses in Montreal, one in Toronto, one in Hamilton, one in Port Arthur, one in Winnipeg and one in Vancouver.

This country must protect itself against the advocacy of assassination or violence to the officials of the government of Canada. There must be some law whereby those foreigners who come in here-even if they come from Great Britain because of having been born there-sent in by the Soviet for the purpose of advocating such measures-can be prevented from carrying out their designs. This country must be in a position to protect itself. There is no doubt about that in my mind. If the present enactment goes too far or if it is unjust let us consider some amendment or modification of it. We have other safeguards
under the law.

That is not the method I advocate in dealing with people of that type.

If I may interrupt my hon. friend, I find that I am still right. Let me quote from the act:
Canadian domicile can be acquired for the purpose of this act by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada.
So I was not far wrong in my first statement.
That is one way out, but very narrow.

Let me give another illustration which I think will come home to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, because it is connected with British Columbia, and I think it meets exactly the argument of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. We know there is a very sad and serious and disgraceful condition of affairs in British Columbia in the selling of what is known as dope, especially to children and young people, so much so that this House was moved, on the representations of hon. gentlemen like the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and others from that province, to pass an act 32649-134i
declaring that all those caught selling or dealing in dope would be not only punishable by heavy imprisonment but after conviction would be subject to deportation. I have never heard anyone say there was anything wrong with deportation under those circumstances, because it was preceded by a conviction for a serious offence. It is the very procedure that we seek to apply in these cases of sedition, or alleged sedition, or suspected sedition-try them, convict them if they have committed the crime they are charged with, and then by all means deport them. But give them a trial by a jury of their peers. Both the members for Vancouver Centre and the member for St. Lawrence-St. George, while they uphold the present act to a certain extent, I think suggest some modification. Even the latter admitted that he was willing to make some concession along the lines I have indicated.
The hon. member for West Calgary with that facility so characteristic of him, drew a word picture of an alien agitator:	What
should we do with him? Get rid of him without trial or trouble. What is the use of making a hero of him in the courts? But I would remind the hon. member that we do not make heroes of our criminals, although that may be done elsewhere. It does not put much of a halo around a man if he is committed to the penitentiary for two years and is then deported. You cannot right an injustice by another injustice. I recall the case of a ruler in Turkey who, discovering that one of his subjects, a baker, was selling bread underweight, had him put into his oven and baked with his bread. The potentate boasted that this drastic remedy sufficed to stop the practice! But that is not the way civilized nations enforce their laws. Let us be logical. Let us go back along the lines advocated on the floor of this House to-day, because once you start on a course, whether forward or backward, there is always an ultimate conclusion, if you can arrive at it. Let us go back towards this line of feudalism and medievalism, and where will we land? Before very long we will reach the situation that obtained in France before the revolution, when lettres de cachet were common-I was almost going to say, were saleable; at least they were easily obtained. A royal mistress or other court favourite would get the king or some high official to issue a lettre de cachet, which simply meant a blank warrant of commitment to the Bastile. Very often these blank warrants were issued at night under the influence of passion or liquor, and by the morning the official forgot that he had ever

Immigration Act-Mr. Neill
issued them. Being issued in blank it was open to the political favourite or mistress who had a grudge against some person to fill in that person's name, and the wretched victim was consigned to the Bastile without the formality of a trial. I emphasize that-without the formality of a trial. When the Bastile was taken by the revolutionists it was found that a large number of those immured there did not themselves know why they had been imprisoned. The parties who had obtained the lettres de cachet had died, their poor victims were forgotten, and remained entombed. That is only carrying the principle suggested to-day a little further backward.
It is a truism in political history that those who seek to forward the cause of progress and to uplift the status of the common people have to be ever on the watch against those who desire to turn the clock of progress back to the days which they fondly hope may yet return, and to revive the principles of reaction. This might be called perhaps an absurd comparison, but a few days ago this House lent itself to the restriction of free speech, and now we are being invited to restrict the liberty of free trial. It simply means going a few more steps backward. Why was not this question brought up last year and debated, why were not the arguments now advanced used then? Because, Mr. Speaker, an election was in sight, and those opposing this bill had to answer to the common people, so they did not think it advisable to take their present stand. But now an election is far away and it is hoped perhaps to make a few steps backward. It is natural for hon. members of a certain profession to take a retrograde step. They are proverbially the slaves of precedent; they are always looking behind them rather than forward.
I propose to vote for this bill, not because it encourages bolshevism. It does not. It is a bulwark against bolshevism, for you cannot right one wrong with another. I believe the best protection against bolshevism is to give freedom-certainly freedom of trial. I object to these clauses of the Immigration Act, not because of the deportation feature -deport everyone you like-but I do firmly and consistently object to the system of deportation without trial. That is the crux of my argument. Our forebears obtained the right of free trial by our peers on the field of Runnymede from King John. That is a long time ago. And it ill behooves us to take any steps, however slight, to deprive Canadian citizens of that right.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very
brief, but I think before the House is called upon to vote on this bill we should examine it in its true light. It is not my intention to answer the appeals, very eloquent, it is true, that have been made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), but I shall try and explain in a few sentences just what this bill means, and what its effect will be if it is adopted.
When an immigrant comes to Canada, according to our existing laws he is examined .when he is seeking entry. He is either passed as a desirable citizen, or else the officials of the department refuse him entry, and that ends his case. But if he enters Canada, the immigration authorities still maintain control over him after he has entered, and that control can be exercised in two ways. It may be exercised in exceptional cases by way of direct deportation after a board has given a decision on the case. I may say that that method should not be used unless the circumstances warrant it, and those circumstances must be of a most abnormal character. The second way of dealing with the immigrant who has already entered Canada, and who has become after his entry an undesirable citizen, is to convict him in court of a criminal offence, and after conviction deport him.
Was that always necessary?

I am giving the general
lines of the law; I am not going into details. Last year this bill was introduced. It was fully discussed, and finally passed this House. This year it is again introduced, and we hear three main opponents of the bill-the hon. member for West Calgary, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). First of all I might call the attention of the House to the law as it exists, not a law that I might build up with a view to making a good argument, but the law as it is in our statutes to-day.
I would call the attention of hon. members to section 2 of the Immigration Act. My hon. friend the member for Vancouver Centre has spoken of the act of 1910. I now hold in my hand the law as it exists to-day, in 1927, and let us examine the law as it is to-day, and as it has been enacted by parliament. The law of the land to-day, in section 2, defines what an undesirable is, and if my hon, friend from Vancouver Centre will read the definition of an undesirable to be found in that section, he will find that the immigration authorities have complete authority to exclude from this

Immigration Act-Mr. Cannon
country any person who would not be a citizen that Canada would like to 'have within its boundaries. I say, first, that the department has full authority to-day to keep out of Canada whomsoever they wish to keep out.
Now take the case of a British subject born in England who comes to Canada. Under the section which we are now seeking to repeal, that British subject has been placed by the amendment of 1919 in a position of exception. A Doukhobor who has come to Canada and become a naturalized citizen cannot be deported under the law of 1919, but a British subject born in England, even though he had lived here for twenty-five or thirty years, is deportable under section 41. The hon. member for West Calgary appealed to the House this morning on behalf of British citizenship. Is it fair for the parliament of a British dominion to leave on the statute book a law which says that a British subject born outside of Canada shall be deported, while a foreigner born in Russia who has acquired Canadian citizenship through naturalization shall hot be touched under the same circumstances? That is the point, and that is the law we are asking the House to repeal.
Why not amend it?

We amend the law when
there is something good in it; we repeal it when it is all wrong. According to the law passed in 1919, this parliament gave to the immigration authorities an exceptional power, and that exceptional power was directed against British citizens bom outside of Canada. It has been asked, if British citizens come into Canada and commit offences against (he state, is that a reason why they should not be deported? In answer to that I am not asking that the British citizen born outside of Canada should not be treated as they ought to be treated when they commit offences, but I say that under our law they should be placed on a parity with the other citizens of Canadh, and in asking this House to repea1 this law we are simply asking that they be treated by the immigration authorities as any other person who has entered Canada would be treated under the like circumstances. Is that fair? Can there be any objection to it? When my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre and my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George appeal to this House against this bill by describing the attempts of the bolsheviks in Canada to overthrow this government, my answer to that is simply that we can deal with the bolsheviks now under the existing law. But the section we are repealing here is a section which is directed against British citizens, not against Russians, not against
bolsheviks. If you want to deal with bolsheviks or with people who come here from central Europe and have revolutionary ideas, you have power under section 40 to deal with them, but if you want to deal with British subjects and d'eport them at will in an arbitrary way, depriving them even of the right of appeal to a court to claim the liberty and freedom which they had as British subjects in England, so long as section 41 is on the statute book of Canada, an arbitrary Minister of Immigration can deport them ta England without giving them a hearing in. court or anywhere else.

May I ask a question?
Paragraphs (n) and1 (o) of section 3 of the act deal with persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Canada, or persons who are members of or are affiliated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief or opposition to organized government. Now, is it not competent for the Minister of Immigration, without trial, without reference to any court, without conviction, to deport persons who come under these two paragraphs, whether they be British subjects or aliens other than persons with a Canadian domicile of at least five years?
I was waiting for my hon. friend right there. If such be the case, section 41 is not necessary, so why oppose this bill?

For this reason, that section 41 contains other offences of a similar character that are not included' in these two paragraphs, and furthermore, I might add that we have repeatedly asked for the restoration of section 41 of the act of 1910 and the dropping of this present section.

My hon. friend says: If
you put in the adt section 41 of the act of 1910, I have no objection. But this morning my hon. friend stated to the House that his objection to section 41 as it is to-day was that it would allow the deportation of people who were even suspected or reputed to be members of an illegal or unlawful association.

I did not say that, What I said was that if it would help the matter, then as far as I was concerned I would agree to the deletion of those words "who by common repute belongs to or is suspected of belonging" and so forth.

The moment you delete
those words from section 41, there is no difference of any importance between, section 40 and section 41.

Oh, yes.

Immigration Act-Mr. Cannon

Is section
40 very long? If not, I would ask the Solicitor General to be good enough to read it.

I wish hon. members to bear in mind that if we should pass this bili section 40 remains untouched. What does section 40 say? It reads:
Whenever any person, other than a Canadian citizen or person having Canadian domicile shall be found an inmate of or connected with the management of a house of prostitution, or practising prostitution or who shall receive, share in, or derive benefit from any part of the earnings of any prostitute or who manages or is employed by, in, or in connection with any house of prostitution or music or dance hall or other place of amusement or resort habitually frequented by prostitutes, or where prostitutes gather, or who in any way assists any prostitute or protects or promises to protect from arrest any prostitute or who shall import or attempt to import any person for the purpose of prostitution or for any other immoral purpose, or who has been convicted of a criminal offence in Canada-
Any of these things.
-or who admits the commission prior to landing or entry to Canada of a crime involving moral turpitude, or has become a professional beggar or a public charge or practices polygamy, or has become an inmate of a penitentiary, gaol, reformatory, prison, asylum or hospital for the insane or the mentally deficient, or an inmate of a public charitable institution, or enters or remains in Canada contrary to any provision of this act, it shall be the duty of any officer cognizant thereof, and the duty of the clerk, secretary, or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein such person may be, to forthwith send a written complaint thereof to the minister, giving full particulars.
I call the attention of the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) to the words:
-or enters or remains in Canada contrary to any provision of this act.
This means that, according to section 3, any persons who belong to the prohibited class enumerated in clause 3, even though they have entered Canada, even though they may be in Canada, fall under section 3 of the act, and they would be in Canada against the provisions of the act, and would therefore be liable to be dealt with under section 40. I think, Mr. Speaker, that section 40 gives the power to deal with all cases under normal conditions. Section 41, I understood, was brought into our law under exceptional conditions, with which I do not wish to deal.
No, it was amended only. It was brought in in 1910.
The section as it stands to-day is the section enacted in 1919.
Amended only.

In 1919 section 41 was introduced in parliament. I do not wish to discuss the question whether the government of the time was justified in introducing it or not. These events are now past, and I do not wish to re-open the debate upon them.

I was seeking to find out whether, after the repeal of this section, there would be anything left in the act by which you could get after those who are referred to as undertaking to break down constituted authority, and that sort of thing.
Has the hon. member the act before him?
No.

I ask my hon. friend to
refer to clause 3 of the act, paragraphs (n) and (o), which read as follows:
(n)	Persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Canaua or of constituted law and authority, or who disbelieve in or are opposed to organized government, or who advocate the assassination of public officials, or who advocate or teach the unlawful destruction of property.
These people can be dealt with under section 40. Then paragraph (o) reads:
(o)	Persons who are members of or affiliated with any organization entertaining or teaching disbelief in or opposition to organized government, or advocating or teaching the duty, necessity, or propriety of the unlawful assaulting or killing of any officer or officers, either of specific individuals or of officers generally, of the government of Canada or of any other organized government, because of his or their official character, or advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property.
I think I am justified in concluding that even though section 41 be repealed, we have provisions in the law which would enable the government to deal with all these cases in a very satisfactory way. My interpretation may be questioned, but in order to relieve the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, I will quote the opinion of the hon. member for West Calgary. When this legislation was considered last year I took part in the debate, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) being present. I "would call the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre particularly to this because I know he has great confidence in the hon. member for West Calgary as a lawyer.
He is usually right.

This is what took place:
Mr. Cannon: Section 40 covers the case.

Immigration Act-Mr. Ryckman
That is what I argued last year and it is whait I am arguing now.
Mr. Lapointe: I agree that section 40 would cover the case, and the only purpose of the bill would be to repeal section 41.
Mr. Bennett: The new section is of no value at all.
Is that a question?

No, it is a statement from the hon. member for West Calgary who was heard in the House this morning denouncing this bill in such violent terms and asking hon. members to reject it on the ground that it would mean the overthrow of any form of decent government and of democracy in Canada. Last year, however, he declared that section 41 was of no value at all. I leave the bill in the hands of the House confident that, in view of the advice given by the 'hon. member that section 41 is of no value at all, hon. gentlemen will accept the amendment.

I am driven to my feet by the observations of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) who has taken this opportunity of discussing the subject in the absence of the hon. member for West Calgary. I had not before heaid of this statement attributed to the hon. member for West Calgary when the bill was under consideration on a former occasion. Anyone who has listened to what has just been read by the Solicitor General must come to one of two conclusions-either that the statement that section 41 was of no value at all is an interrogation, or that it was made upon the understanding that the former section 41 was to remain in the act.

To be fair to the hon.
member for West Calgary, I wish to add that after we had reached that conclusion we decided upon the section as now drafted and it met with the hon. gentleman's approval.

I cannot speak as to
that. It is plain that the act as drafted thi3 year is in different terms from the act of last year, and the assumption I had in mind when I first saw the bill was that section 41 of the Immigration Act of 1910 would be restored and become operative. It is however obvious that, if this amendment of 1919 is withdrawn, section 41 of the Immigration Act also disappears. I do not think there need be occasion for any difference of opinion with regard to what is stricken out of the law if this bill passes, but I want to call the attention of the House to the situation, which can be stated very tersely. Whether or not it is a corollary of what took place at the Imperial
conference I do not know, but it seems that the Prime Minister and the government are now satisfied that while the immigration authorities shall retain the power to exclude from Canada or to deport any one who advocates the overthrow of the government of this Dominion, if he advocates the overthrow of the government of Great Britain he shall not be subject to exclusion or deportation.
In other words, we can protect our own government but we are entitled to prevent any man from advocating the overthrow of the government of Great Britain or, say, of Australia. We are certainly enjoying our status to the full.
My hon. friend has not read the law.

If the Solicitor General will pardon me, I will come to the point he has in mind. By this legislation, I say, we can protect ourselves. We can take by the scruff of the neck, if I may use that expression, and throw out of the country any man who advocates or proposes to advocate the overthrow of the government of Canada, but he may advocate with impunity the overthrow of the government of Great Britain and enter the country. I know that the Solicitor General will refer me to the words "constituted authority"; the act provides that we may deal with any one who proposes . to attack constituted authority. But what does that mean? How is it interpreted? It is interpreted in the context in which it is found: it is not constituted authority in any other place than Canada. Would the Solicitor General say that the constituted authority of the Fiji islands was protected by this provision? Of course not. Nor can you say that the constituted authority of Great Britain is protected to any greater extent.
I did not mention constituted authority alone; I read the law as it is.
Organized government.
The law says, "any government of Canada or any other organized government ". That includes the government of Great Britain.
Read beyond that clause; that refers only to the assassination of officials.
I suggest that before the Solicitor General attempts to interpret the law in relation to this most important subject, he should read it.

I have read it; I have read more of it than my hon. friend.
2124	COMMONS
Immigration Act-Mr. Ryckman

I say now to the Solicitor General that the part of the section he has read does not refer to constituted government, other than the government of Canada, except in connection with the specific purpose mentioned. Now this is the legislation which the Prime Minister is asking us to pass. I am absolutely opposed to it. There is no country we admire anywhere on the face of the globe which has not the right to forbid the entry of undesirable immigrants who show anarchistic tendencies. What does Great Britain do? At the Channel ports there are two officers of Scotland Yard who inspect passengers as they land, and if there is anyone whom they suspect of harbouring such tendencies they ask him to justify himself; otherwise they put him back on the boat and deport him. And there is not an hon. member who will not approve of that course. The Solicitor General says that we control our immigrants. Of course we do. But unless we retain the provision which it is now' being sought to repeal we have no control over the man who comes with a passport and who we know is seeking to destroy the constituted authority of Great Britain. That I submit is a privilege we do not wish to forego. And I for one stand resolutely for it. The Solicitor General referred by way of contrast to a Doukhobor and to British citizens. And who was the Doukhobor to whom he referred? It was a Doukhobor who had been crowned with Canadian citizenship, and the hon. member compared him to a British subject who had no Canadian citizenship. I say that this parliament gives credit to the man who has Canadian citizenship, no matter where he was born or what his extraction. That is why there is this distinction.

Does my hon. friend
mean that I am not a Canadian citizen? He draws that distinction between a British subject and a Canadian citizen, and says that a Canadian citizen has greater rights than a British subject.

I say that a Canadian
citizen has greater rights in Canada than some British subjects.
We do not think so. I would like the opinion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on that point.

My hon. friend is a lawyer. In order to complete his argument will he point out by what method a British subject bom in England would acquire Canadian citizenship?
[Mr. Cannon.)
Yes; how can I become a Canadian?

How can he do it? My
hon. friend is a lawyer.

Behave
yourself for a while.
It is hard to do with this kind of talk.
Answer my question.

Give me time, and you will very soon get an answer. I will tell the House what a Canadian citizen is, and I will tell the Solicitor General that when he was objecting to what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre had said he did not read everything. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) read one section; the Solicitor General read the next section, but he did not read the third section. Why did he not give the whole interpretation of "Canadian citizen" as set out by the act? Let us have the whole thing read.

I will say one thing to
my hon. friend in order that we may not disagree, further. If he wants to argue fairly I will do so, but if my hon. friend does not want to be fair I will not discuss it at all. I have been fair all through with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, and I am not used to these methods.

I have no quarrel except with the argument of the Solicitor General. I certainly desire to be fair and I want to read everything that is included in the definition of a Canadian citizen, which has not yet, been given to the House. A Canadian citizen means a person born in Canada who has not become an alien; that was read by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Or a Canadian citizen means a British subject who has Canadian domicile; that was read by the Solicitor General.
Then I am all right.

In that one particular
you are all right. The part which was not read says that a Canadian citizen is one naturalized under the laws of Canada who has not subsequently become an alien or lost Canadian domicile.

Now read the definition
of "domicile".

That is the whole of
that definition.

If my hon. friend will
allow me, these are very complicated matters.

Immigration Act-Mr. Ryckman

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that if this bill passes it will be possible for men to land on our shores for the purpose of attacking the British Empire and the overseas dominions, and to carry on their machinations here. Section 40, the prostitution clause as I call it, does not cover this case, and no man of repute on either side of the House will say that it does. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that an unfair tone has been given the discussion by the introduction of a slogan which has been uttered more than once; "Oh, deportation without trial is not right". We have the privilege, which I think the Solicitor General will not deny, of turning back an immigrant who desires to land or who may even have his feet on our shores, because he is not desirable. That is deportation without trial. No man values more than I do the necessity of giving a fair trial to any Canadian citizen within our shores who has offended against the law or who is supposed to have offended in that way. He is entitled to that, even though it puts the country to an expense which sometimes is very heavy; that is quite proper. It certainly is not proper, however, that the machinery of our courts should be called upon at such expense to try men whom we know come here determined to destroy the government, anarchists and such like, instead of building up constituted authority throughout the world.

Would the hon.
gentleman say which is the most serious, to attack the British Empire or to attack British rights?

I must frankly admit that I do not understand the question, because British rights are not available to the man who comes here seeking to destroy British authority; the House will admit that. There was a member of the British House of Commons, a man named Saklatvala, who admitted that he was against all constituted authority unless perhaps a soviet might be termed such. He sought to enter the United States; he was a man of ability and a member of the British House but his views were well known and he never got beyond Ellis Island. I do not think more than a dozen members of this House would say that he had a right to get any further. These problems will confront us, and we must be able to deal with them; we must deal with them as Great Britain does. When an anarchist is found seeking entry into Great Britain, Scotland Yard is there to send him right back; he has no chance and is not entitled to one. British
law everywhere gives a Britisher or any decent foreigner a chance to establish his rights, but when they know a man has denied himself the privileges of a British citizen, then he does not get anything but short shrift. That is the essence of British law.
May I ask if Scotland Yard was on hand to send Saklatvala back, to India?
If the hon. member had been listening he would have heard me put the locale as Ellis Island; the United States sent him back.
But did Scotland Yard immediately ship this man back to India?

He was dealt with by the immigration authorities and got no further than Ellis Island. He had no chance to spread his propaganda in the United States, and we ought to put ourselves in the same position. Anyone who wants to indulge in propaganda against Great Britain and her people should not be allowed to come into the country, which is a part of the British Empire.

Was that gentleman
allowed to enter England on his return? When he was sent back from Ellis Island did they permit him to enter England?

I presume he was as a
British subject. And I want to tell hon. gentlemen that a Canadian citizen, who was born in this country and has lived here, or a Canadian citizen by naturalization, is entitled, if he leaves Canada, to come back to it from any quarter of the globe, unless he has broken the laws of the land.
May I suggest that Mr. Saklatvala was not born in England, he was born in India.
* But he was a British subject.

Is the hon. gentleman
suggesting that we should change our law and adopt that of the United States?

I prefer not to answer
questions put by the hon. member for Temis-couata always under great heat.
I shall not detain the House further. I think that at this time it would be improper to cut out this section in the wholesale way that is proposed. I think the majority of this House are of one mind. We want to give fair treatment to everyone but we do not want to discriminate at the present time-* especially so soon after the Imperial con-

Immigration Act-Mr. Guthrie
ferenoe of which we have heard so much- against other portions of the British Empire. That does not comport with our new status, it does not conduce to inter-imperial good will and inter-imperial relations. I ask the House to consider this question, and that each member put it to himself: is he prepared to allow our immigration authorities to say to the man who is plotting against the government of Canada "You cannot come in, but if you are plotting against the government of Great Britain you can?"

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Before this motion is carried
there are one or two things I should like to point out. The Immigration Act which obtained in this country in 1910 was one which was passed by this parliament at a time of peace. We had no difficulties of any kind in Canada, and we had no difficulties in foreign countries. If I remember correctly, the bill of 1910 passed this House without arousing opposition and, I think, without division. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister was in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time, the government that passed the act. I think he occupied at that time the position of Minister of Labour. I too was a supporter of the bill of 1910 and I think it was generally supported in the House and in the country. Now that act had been in force-there may have been some amendments to it, but I do not think there were any-until the year 1919 when, on account of the circumstances in which we found ourselves at the end of the war, it became necessary to enact provisions more drastic than ever had been in the act of 1910. Sections 40 and 41 which appeared in the act of 1910 reappeared in the act of 1919 but in different form. They were amplified, they were made broader in their application in many ways. It was thought well by the parliament of that day to do this owing to the peculiar circumstances in which we found ourselves at the time of the great conflict and which were so well described to the House to-day by my hon. friend from St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan). However, several years have passed since the year 1919. I do not pretend to say that the situation in Canada to-day resembles in any respect the situation which existed when the act of 1919 was passed. But I do say that the situation which exists in Canada to-day very much resembles the situation which existed in 1910 when the Immigration Act was passed. Now that act worked well. It would work well to-day. Why not settle this dispute by reverting to the provisions of the act of 1910? In my
FMr. Ryckman.]
judgment it provided all the safeguards necessary then. It would provide all the safeguards necessary to-day. But I am going to point out this fact just here. My hon. friend the Solicitor General has entirely misapprehended the effect of the present act, that is the act of 1919, which the government seeks to repeal by this bill. He has misapprehended the meaning of the sections which he read to the House a few minutes ago. He only read part of those sections. I maintain that in section 41 of the act of 1919 there are provisions which will not appear in our immigration law if that section is repealed. There was a difference of opinion between my hon. friend and the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) a moment ago, and it merely involved the single question as to whether subsections (n) and (o) made provision against persons who attempted crimes against the government of this country, and possibly of other countries. It will be remembered that section 41 does make such provision. Section 41 is a very broad and comprehensive section. It provides:
(1) Every person who by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or Canada, or any of the provinces of Canada, or the government of any other of His Majesty's dominions, colonies, possessions or dependencies, or advocates the assassination of any official of any of the said governments or of any foreign government, or who in Canada defends

And so on. I do not need to read the balance of the section. Now if that section is repealed we are left then to subsections (n) and (o) of section 3 of the act which deal with prohibited classes subject to deportation. I am not asking any special consideration for this bill or for this company, because I apprehend that hon. gentlemen who know something of the history of the company will let its actions, its statements and its officials speak for it, which makes it unnecessary for me to present any brief. The whole contention seems to have centred upon a determination of the capital of this company, in, which connection a brief has been submitted to the officials of the iSun Life Assurance Company by a very eminent counsel, assuring them that no action on the part of this government is necessary to make it certain that the capital is already $4,000,000, the amount asked. In all fairness to the committee and to the company, these contentious matters could have been better worked out, I think, in that small select committee than in this House.

When you consider that the interest of the policyholders in this company is a little over 99 per cent, it will be appreciated that those who control no more than one per cent of the assets are asking a lot when they request the right to double their capital, which would doubtless be done by the issuance of shares, commonly called watered stock. The construction of the railway is the simplest part of the work from the point of view of time. A large part of the study given to this subject by the officers of the government has been directed towards the most expeditious and economical method of port development. In connection with Port Nelson the feature which is the greatest time consumer is the necessity for dredging a portion of the channel. The natural channel extends up the estuary of the Nelson. The artificial island which is now partly constructed is some twenty-two miles from the bay itself and a navigable channel of sufficient depth extends to within approximately five miles of that island. For three and a half miles of that last five, the channel must
be dredged. That has been well known for a number of years. The amount of dredging required is approximately five and a half million cubic yards in a channel three hundred feet wide and approximately three and a half miles long, varying in depth. At any rate the work involves the removal of five and a half million cubic yards of material.
What kind of bottom?

The nature of the material is boulder clay which can be disposed of with a dipper dredge. That is the great time consumer in connection with Nelson. There is no doubt at all that we can complete the railway and the necessary dock and terminal facilities very much sooner than it would be possible for ships to come up to the dock, the reason being, as I have stated, the fact that so much dredging requires to be done. The department has been at some considerable trouble to estimate the length of time which will be necessary in order to accomplish this dredging. Of necessity, estimates of this character must be only approximate, inasmuch as delay may occur through breakage of machinery and operating under water. Another factor to be considered is this: the material dredged must be transported by scows over the twenty-two miles to the open sea or bay. It cannot be dumped in the channel or in the shallow water because the tendency would be to block the channel lower down. It is necessary therefore to plan not only the dredging of the artificial channel to which I am referring but to carry the dredged material twenty-two miles out to the sea. On the basis of operating these dredges with the necessary auxiliary craft the period estimated by the department's engineers before the complete channel up to the dock will be fully available for use will be six years. That does not mean that the port cannot be used at all before the lapse of that time. It may be possible to use the channel before it is dredged to its ultimate width but there are of course necessary limitations to such use. When the government was made aware of the study which the engineers had given to this phase of the subject it was deemed desirable, having regard to the need of getting operations started as expeditiously as possible, to secure the very best advice on port development. It was recognized, in view of the controversial nature of the Hudson bay project, that if any Canadian engineer were invited to make a study of it in all probability there would be charges or statements that he was prejudiced one way or the other; therefore the government decided to endeavour to secure the services of

an unquestioned authority on port development. Through the cooperation of the High Commissioner in London the services of Mr. Frederick Palmer were secured for that work. Who is Mr. Palmer? Mr. Frederick Palmer is an engineer of long and wide experience in port development in many parts of the world; he was for many years chief engineer for the government of India in connection with railways, ports and irrigation; more recently he has been the head of his own firm in London; at present he is consulting engineer to the ports of London and Glasgow and is consulting engineer to. the British government in connection with colonial port development. This year he also occupies what I believe is regarded as the blue ribbon position of the engineering world; he is president of the British Engineering Institute. I think there can be no question that in securing the advice of such a man in connection with an undertaking involving such large expenditures, the government has adopted a wise course. Mr. Palmer visited Ottawa and conducted here an examination of all the records and data in connection with the Hudson bay project; he will return in the summer to pay a personal visit to Hudson bay. Following consultation with him and after he had gone into the records very considerably, on behalf of the government I wrote him a letter of instruction which I propose to read to the committee, in order that the position of things from the point of view of the government's instructions to the engineer may be plain. The letter is dated January 5, 1927, and is as follows:
Dear Mr. Palmek,
In order that we may have record of the understandings reached as a result of our several conferences, I beg to advise you as follows:
In 1911, the Canadian government commenced the construction of a railway to Hudson bay. In 1912, in order that the road might be placed completely under contract, it became necessary for the government of the day to make immediate choice between the only two possible ports on the west coast, Nelson and Churchill. After a personal visit to both places by the then minister, and consideration of the information available at the time, the minister, on the advice of his engineering staff, recommended the establishment of the railway terminus at Nelson. and plans for harbour terminals were prepared by an engineer specially selected and sent to Nelson for that purpose. Upon consideration of the scheme of development then suggested differences of opinion arose, and the engineer resigned his appointment. A member of the departmental engineering staff was then assigned the task of preparing suitable plans, as a result of which the present scheme of development at Nelson was approved and actively prosecuted by the department during 1914 and the succeeding years, until the fall of 1917, when the work was discontinued owing to war con-
ditions. During the following winter the construction of the railway was also discontinued upon completion of the bridge at the Kettle rapids crossing of the Nelson river, about 92 miles from Port Nelson.
On the railway $15,245,889 had been expended to March 31, 1926, and on the Nelson terminals $6,242,114.
At the present time that portion of the railway previously constructed is being reconditioned and it is planned to continue the construction of the railway in 1927. This imposes upon the government early consideration of the question of harbour development in order that the Hudson bay route may be assured fair trial as an ocean outlet for western grain and cattle, and for such other traffic in agricultural, mineral, forest and manufactured products as may develop.
Controversy has always existed as to the relative merits of Nelson and Churchill as the bay terminus, and notwithstanding the selection of Nelson in 1912-13, controversy has persisted. In 1920, a special committee of the Senate was appointed to examine and report upon the Hudson bay project generally, and upon the character of the ports and their fitness for terminals. Upon the evidence then adduced the committee reached the following conclusion upon the harbour phase of the project:
"That in the opinion of this committee sufficient care was not taken in the selection of Nelson as the terminus of the railway, and that the government should not make further important expenditures upon this port without first making a new and thorough examination into the relative merits of Churchill and Nelson as a terminus for the railroad."
In view of the substantial expenditure already incurred at Nelson, and the shorter rail haul to that point, the government is naturally predisposed towards Nelson, but desires, above all things, that the port chosen, and its arrangements, should afford the best possible opportunity for the development of trade through the bay.
The problem of harbour development in the two places differs very widely and, as regards Churchill, the use of that port would involve the construction, maintenance and operation of about 90 additional miles of railway. As to the suitability of the terrain between the Nelson and the Churchill rivers to railway construction *we hope to have definite information in the course of the next few months. Should the survey now being made disclose conditions unfavourable to railway construction, this would, of course, dispose of any question as to Churchill, but if a railway is found practicable, we will require your advice concerning Churchill also. If that port should be found to be capable of such early and economic development as would afford better and safer facilities than Nelson, and more readily available, that would be a factor of great importance to the successful development of the Hudson bay route. For these reasons we think it unwise and not in the interests of Canada to restrict your investigation to the port of Nelson only, unless, meanwhile, Churchill should be eliminated for railway reasons.
In the event of Churchill becoming a possibility we should have, in addition to relative costs of construction and maintenance, a comparative estimate of the length of time neces-

Supply-Hudson Bay Railway
sary to provide terminals at either port sufficient to enable a proper test of the route to be made. We consider this element of time a matter of prime importance.
We want, also your opinion of the design of the existing works at Nelson, and as to whether any change could be made there which would either reduce the cost or the length of time required for deve'opment, or improve conditions in any way at that point.
What we have in mind as an initial test development-and this is suggested more for your guidance than as a conclusive and limiting instruction-would be the provision of accommodation in either harbour for six cargo ships in port at one time, with working berth for three of the six, the estimated draft of vessels to be not less than 26 feet. The minimum development projected at each port should, of course, be capable of such progressive extension as future requirements might dictate.
If a railway to Churchill be found practicable, we desire that your report should cover a possible development at both Nelson and Churchill, with estimated cost, your recommendation as to the choice to be made and reasons therefor.
In outlining, in this general way, the matters upon which the government desires your advice, it is not intended to ask you to consider problems unconnected with port development. We appreciate that, owing to climatic conditions, it will not be possible for you to conduct your personal examination of Nelson and Churchill before next summer. We shall, however, do everything in our power to facilitate your work at both points and would be glad to have your conclusions as soon as possible thereafter, as we are anxious to avoid delay in the prosecution of this important undertaking.
Faithfully yours,
Charles A. Dunning.

One question

Supply-Railways and Canals
understand a committee has been appointed consisting of three representatives, one from the Department of Railways, another from the Department of Public Works, and a third representing the railways, to consider the location of the terminal port. I am interested, of course, in the town of Brockville. There are other points that are interested in the same matter, namely, Kingston and Prescott. Will the location of this terminal be in any way affected by the size, the number, the personnel, or the political complexion of delegations who wait upon the department, or will it have regard to the respective advantages of these particular places? I would hope that it would be disposed of on the basis of the economic merits of the different places.

I think my hon. friend is aware of the answers which as minister I have given to several of the delegations to which my hon. friend has referred. The answer is that we are not determining this question on the basis of representations made by those representing very worthily particular localities which are naturally looking after their interests to the best of their ability, but rather on the basis of an economic study. I think my hon. friend is familiar with the important questions involved,' as they relate to the trade of Canada, particularly in the transportation sense, and it is the endeavour of the department concerned to deal with it on that basis, and having regard to that factor only.

That is quite
satisfactory.

As to what may be done, it is a little early yet to indicate. But if as a result of what is determined upon, it is necessary for the Department of Railways and Canals to do anything this year, we can utilize a portion of the fund now voted for the Welland canal, because any work which is done is really a continuation of the Welland canal. We do not expect however, during the current fiscal year any expenditure under this head to amount to anything.
When does the minister expect to have the information which will enable the government to decide the location of the terminal?
It will be two or three months in any event.
That is satisfactory.

And it is not a matter we should jump at, because the Welland canal will not be completed until 1930 if we keep up our present schedule. But it was thought desirable to investigate thoroughly this other important factor before the completion of the Welland canal.

What is the estimated
total cost up to and including 1930?

What has been spent
up to the present time?

What is the cost to
date?

include interest on the money spent all these years, or is it for bare expenditures?
Just expenditures.

The money is paid by the Department of Finance from time to time. We have in our department no calculation of the interest.

The minister made a remark regarding which I wish to have an explanation. I understood him to say that out of this vote of $14,500,000 which we are now making for the Welland, ship canal construction there would be enough to provide for work in connection with lake terminals if necessary.

I did not mean to amply that. I meant rather that any necessary preparatory work, the taking of bearings for example, the determination of the nature of the works and any incidental expenses of that character would be taken care of out of this vote. We could not of course without coming to parliament spend the money on work in connection with the terminals.

I question very much
whether you could take any money for the purpose out of this vote. What would the Auditor General say if you did?

If he decides that we
cannot, then that settles it.

Supply-Railways and Canals

If the money is voted for the Welland canal construction that is the only purpose for which it can be used. I have always been under the impression that money voted in that way could not be used for any other purpose.
In mentioning the matter I had in mind preliminary work at the eastern end of the Welland canal.

What about work 'at
Kingston or Brockville, say?

H the Auditor General objects we cannot spend the money. One of my objects in mentioning the matter was to make it clear to the committee that it was our intention to move forward and secure actual data upon which to base conclusions in the future.
You would have to take it out of miscellaneous.
Perhaps so.
Unless the rules in the Auditor General's department have been relaxed, I do not think you could spend the money in this way. In former days we were held strictly to account in matters of this kind.

The Auditor General
holds me just as strictly to account and I do not expect to get past him. I thought however that reference to the matter in parliament might clarify the situation in that regard.
Is the new Welland canal being built on a scale which will enable it to fit in with the larger scheme of deepening the St. Lawrence?
Yes, or rather it is the other way. Unfortunately the Welland canal is larger than the capacity of the other waterway. Our engineers insist that the Welland is taken as a model for the other scheme.
Will the Welland canal be required after the larger scheme is completed?

There may be considerable argument as to the degree of requirement. It will move the present head of deep water navigation from Port Colbome to some other port. As to where that point will be is a matter for inquiry and decision later on. But our largest lake vessels will find it possible to go, instead of to Buffalo or to Port Colborne as at present, through the Welland and up to the eastern end of lake Ontario.

Would there be any
saving as between the fixed charges on the new Welland canal and the extra cost of handling through the present canal?
My hon. friend forgets that we do not charge anything for canal operation. Canada operates the canal and gives the service free.

It must cost something even if the service is given free. Will the fixed charges in connection with the new Welland canal be any greater than the cost involved in this free service of which the minister speaks?
Obviously, of course, you cannot spend $115,000,000 without creating higher fixed charges than were paid before that money was spent.
That is not the point. Will there be any saving as a result of the construction of the new canal? By virtue of the new canal being larger, will the saving be equal to the fixed charges?

I cannot agree with my hon. friend if he says that is the point. No one not gifted with prophecy could possibly answer^ this question. The present Welland canal is congested to the very last degree, and besides, it is too shallow.

What is
the depth of the new canal?
Twenty-five feet. The locks are thirty.

When the new Welland canal was first projected certain estimates were made of economies in freight rates on grain and other commodities. Nlo doubt the minister has those estimates on file in his office; he may possibly have them with him to-might. It would be interesting to find out what saving it is expected will be made in consequence of the deepening of the canal.

I have not the information here. I admit its bearing upon the project as at first introduced, but I suggest that once we have spent $75,000,000 in the undertaking we cannot leave it incomplete. The question is whether we shall finish it or abandon the work that has already been done. We cannot take advantage of that work unless we complete the project, and we cannot continue using the present canal indefinitely. The present canal is being maintained on an operating basis in anticipation of the completion of the new one.

Supply-Railways and Canals
What differences will there be between the new canal and the present waterway in regard to locks?
The difference will be eight locks as against twenty-six, and eight hours instead of fifteen in the passage of vessels through the canal.
Has the minister any information to give in regard to facilities further down the lakes to take care of traffic? What will be the ultimate cost?
What cost?
The cost of the elevators at the points where the new headquarters will be.
That is under consideration at the present moment.
What portion of the canal has already been constructed and how many more years will it be before the work is completed?

The whole work is now
under contract, and we anticipate that it will last another three years.

May I ask the
minister if the department has taken into consideration the length of time required in the- preparation of a terminal, whether temporary or permanent?

Of course I appreciate
my hon. friend's interest; his question is very intelligent, emanating as it does from the hon. member for Kingston, one of the points which would be very materially affected by our decision. The factor to which he refers is being taken into account in the investigation now in progress.

I feel sure that we can trust the minister, but the point I had in mind was that the canal is expected to be open in 1930. Supposing it takes longer than two years to prepare a terminal, what will happen to the traffic going through the canal in the interval between the completion of the canal and the completion of the terminal?
Our engineering advice is that there will be no difficulty in providing the necessary new terminals in the time still available.

The minister says the
canal will not be completed until 1930. I would point out to him that over two billion dollars has been spent on railways in Canada

while only about one-tenth of that amount has been spent on canals. It is very important to the people of Canada that this canal be completed with all convenient speed, because this canal provides most of the revenue so far as the Department of Railways and Canals is concerned. The rapid completion of this canal is of the utmost importance not only to Ontario but to the transportation of the whole Dominion. Last year the old canal handled nearly six million tons, and there has been a yearly increase of twelve and one-half per cent. The work of building the canal has been proceeding since 1913, and we are told now that it will not be finished until 1930, or seventeen years in which to build a canal about twenty-seven miles long. The annual report of the minister is very encouraging with regard to the work accomplished, but I am sorry I have not before me the figures from the Bureau of Statistics. I may tell some of my hon. friends to my left that this is an economic canal and will be a very great help when finished. Therefore I would urge upon the minister the necessity of finishing the construction of this work as rapidly as possible, and to try and complete it before 1930.

In order to answer that
question I will have to read a memorandum I have here, which is as follows:
The discrepancy between the original estimate of cost and the final amount paid is explained as follows: When the survey was made on which the original estimate was based, every effort was made to secure accurate information concerning the rock surface, and from points on the work where solid rock could be definitely located and also from the depth of old crib-work where it could be definitely ascertained, a profile showing the probable rock surface was plotted for the information of intending bidders. After the contract was let, it developed that the probable rock surface, as exhibited, for a length of 250 feet, was a very hard cemented clay intermixed with stones. Consequently the contractors were required to excavate this material to the bottom of the canal for the crib seats, resulting in a large increase in the estimated quantities of excavation, crib-work, stone fulling in cribwork and earth filling behind cribwork.

Would my hon. friend
